(CNN) -- Christine Beatty, chief of staff for former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to charges stemming from their text-messaging sex scandal case and will serve four months in jail, according to the Wayne County prosecutor's office. Under a plea deal, Christine Beatty, shown in August at an arraignment in Detroit, will serve five years probation. Beatty pleaded guilty to two counts of obstruction of justice, according to Maria Miller, the prosecutor's spokeswoman. Charges of perjury and misconduct against Beatty will be dropped as part of the plea arrangement, she said. Beatty agreed to a plea arrangement under which she will serve five years probation -- the first 120 days to be served in jail -- and pay a $100,000 fine, "based on [Beatty's] ability to pay," Miller said. Beatty will begin serving her jail sentence on January 5, when she will be formally sentenced, Miller said. Kym L. Worthy, prosecuting attorney for Wayne County, released a statement saying she is "very pleased that this defendant admitted her guilt." "We live in an age where greed and protecting one's secrets is glorified and accepted," Worthy said. "Now the city of Detroit, the region and the state of Michigan can truly begin to move forward when this ugly chapter in Detroit's history is put to rest." In September, Kilpatrick resigned as mayor and pleaded guilty to two felony obstruction of justice charges stemming from his efforts to cover up his relationship with Beatty. Like Beatty, Kilpatrick was sentenced to five years probation with the first four months to be served in jail. He is serving that sentence in the Wayne County jail. At the time of his sentencing in October, the judge in the case called Kilpatrick "arrogant and defiant," particularly for a televised speech that aired hours after Kilpatrick entered his pleas. "That night, the community expected to hear a message of humility, remorse and apology," Wayne County Circuit Judge David Groner said at Kilpatrick's sentencing. "Instead, we heard an arrogant and defiant man who accused the governor, among others, for his downfall." In addition to his jail and probation sentence, Kilpatrick must also pay the city of Detroit $1 million in restitution, and forfeit any future pension. Initially, Kilpatrick was accused of blocking a criminal investigation into his office and firing a police deputy to cover up an affair with Beatty, then his chief of staff. When that deputy, Gary Brown, filed a whistle-blower suit, Kilpatrick and Beatty denied under oath that an affair had taken place between them. Text messages that contradicted Kilpatrick's and Beatty's denials of an affair were made public in January by the Detroit Free Press, and county prosecutor Worthy charged Kilpatrick and Beatty with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and misconduct in office. The most serious charges would have carried a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison upon conviction. Beatty resigned her post after the text messages were made public. Kilpatrick initially refused to resign after the scandal broke, and Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm called a hearing on whether she should remove him from office at the request of the Detroit City Council. Granholm adjourned those hearings after Kilpatrick pleaded guilty and resigned in September.

**Former Detroit aide Christine Beatty pleads guilty in text-message scandal**

**DETROIT, Michigan (CNN) --** Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff to ex-Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to two felony obstruction-of-justice charges stemming from the text-message scandal that helped force Kilpatrick from office.

Beatty entered the plea in Wayne County Circuit Court, admitting that she gave false testimony during a whistle-blower trial involving two former Detroit police officers. The case centered on whether Beatty and Kilpatrick lied under oath about their personal relationship and their roles in the firing of police officials who had investigated alleged misconduct at City Hall.

The scandal erupted after thousands of text messages published by the *Detroit Free Press* appeared to contradict sworn testimony from both Kilpatrick and Beatty, who had denied having a romantic relationship and denied involvement in the dismissal of the officers.

Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy said Beatty’s plea marked another step in holding public officials accountable.

“This case has never been about private conduct,” Worthy said. “It has been about public corruption, perjury and obstruction of justice.”

Worthy said the prosecution was necessary because officials lied under oath in a civil trial that cost Detroit taxpayers millions of dollars.

“No one is above the law,” Worthy said. “When public officials raise their hands and swear to tell the truth, the citizens have a right to expect that they will do exactly that.”

Beatty’s plea agreement calls for other charges to be dismissed at sentencing. She faces possible jail time, probation, fines and restitution. Sentencing was scheduled for a later date.

Kilpatrick pleaded guilty earlier in the year to obstruction-of-justice charges, agreed to resign as mayor, served jail time and was ordered to pay restitution to the city. His resignation ended a months-long political crisis in Detroit and brought national attention to the text messages between him and Beatty.

The criminal charges grew out of a 2007 whistle-blower lawsuit filed by former police officers Gary Brown and Harold Nelthrope, who alleged they were punished for investigating claims involving the mayor’s security unit. The city ultimately agreed to an $8.4 million settlement with the officers and another former officer.

Prosecutors said the settlement came only after Kilpatrick and Beatty concealed evidence and lied about key facts, including their relationship and their involvement in Brown’s dismissal.

Beatty, once one of Kilpatrick’s closest advisers, resigned from her City Hall post after the text messages became public. In court Monday, she acknowledged her role in obstructing justice but did not make an extended statement.

Worthy said the case should serve as a warning to public servants.

“Truth matters,” she said. “The integrity of the justice system depends on witnesses telling the truth, especially when those witnesses are elected officials or high-ranking public employees.”

**Former Detroit aide pleads guilty as text-message scandal deepens fallout from Kilpatrick administration**

**DETROIT** — Former Detroit Chief of Staff Christine Beatty pleaded guilty Monday to felony obstruction charges, closing another chapter in the text-message scandal that helped topple former Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick and plunged City Hall into months of political crisis.

Beatty’s plea stems from the same controversy that forced Kilpatrick from office earlier this year: thousands of text messages between the mayor and his top aide that appeared to contradict sworn testimony they gave in a police whistleblower trial.

Under the plea agreement, Beatty admitted she obstructed justice in connection with the fallout from the civil case. Prosecutors had accused her and Kilpatrick of lying under oath about both their romantic relationship and their roles in the dismissal or mistreatment of police officials who claimed they were punished for probing alleged misconduct involving the mayor’s security unit.

The scandal began with a lawsuit brought by former Detroit police officers, who alleged they were retaliated against after raising questions about the conduct of Kilpatrick’s security team. During the 2007 trial, both Kilpatrick and Beatty denied having a sexual relationship and denied that the officers had been targeted for political reasons.

But text messages later obtained and published by the *Detroit Free Press* showed intimate exchanges between Kilpatrick and Beatty and included discussions prosecutors said were relevant to the whistleblower litigation. The messages appeared to undercut the pair’s sworn testimony, triggering perjury and obstruction investigations.

Kilpatrick, once considered one of the Democratic Party’s rising urban political figures, pleaded guilty earlier to obstruction of justice and no contest to assault-related charges in a separate case involving sheriff’s deputies. As part of his plea deal, he agreed to resign as mayor, serve jail time, repay the city, surrender his law license, and remain on probation for years.

His resignation marked a stunning fall for a politician who had won office as Detroit’s youngest mayor and had long presented himself as a symbol of the city’s future. Instead, the scandal consumed his administration, damaged public trust, and exposed deep divisions in Detroit politics.

The text-message revelations also raised questions about a multimillion-dollar settlement in the whistleblower lawsuit. Critics alleged the Kilpatrick administration agreed to pay more than $8 million to resolve the officers’ claims in part to keep the damaging messages from becoming public. That issue became central to the criminal investigation, with prosecutors arguing that the alleged deception cost taxpayers and undermined the justice system.

Beatty, who had been one of Kilpatrick’s closest advisers and most powerful figures inside City Hall, left her post after the scandal erupted. Her guilty plea means both key figures at the center of the controversy have now acknowledged criminal wrongdoing tied to the case.

The political fallout in Detroit was immediate and far-reaching. City Council members who had battled Kilpatrick for months over the scandal called for his resignation before his plea. State officials, including Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm, began proceedings that could have removed him from office had he not stepped down. The scandal also intensified scrutiny of city finances, contracting, police oversight and the culture of loyalty surrounding the mayor’s office.

After Kilpatrick’s departure, Detroit moved to install new leadership and restore credibility to city government. But the damage lingered: taxpayers were left with the cost of the whistleblower settlement, officials faced renewed questions about transparency, and residents watched a mayoral administration collapse under the weight of personal misconduct, courtroom lies and political defiance.

Beatty’s plea does not erase the broader controversy, but it represents one of the final legal admissions in the scandal that reshaped Detroit politics and ended Kilpatrick’s tenure in disgrace.

Christine Beatty, former chief of staff to Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty in the Detroit City Hall text-message scandal to felony obstruction-of-justice charges tied to false sworn testimony in a police whistle-blower lawsuit.

## What Beatty admitted

Beatty acknowledged that she gave false testimony under oath during the 2007 whistle-blower trial brought by former Detroit police officers. At trial, both she and Kilpatrick denied having a romantic relationship and denied key allegations about retaliation against police officials. Later-disclosed text messages between Beatty and Kilpatrick contradicted that testimony, showing an intimate relationship and discussions relevant to the firing and treatment of officers.

Her guilty plea centered on obstruction of justice—lying in a legal proceeding in a way that interfered with the administration of justice.

## Background: the whistle-blower lawsuit

The scandal grew out of a lawsuit filed by former Detroit police officers, including Gary Brown and Harold Nelthrope, who claimed they were retaliated against after raising concerns about misconduct and investigations involving the mayor’s security detail and City Hall.

In 2007, a jury awarded the officers more than $6 million. The city later settled the case for $8.4 million. The settlement became explosive because it included efforts to keep the text messages from becoming public—messages that appeared to show Kilpatrick and Beatty had lied under oath.

The Detroit Free Press later obtained and published excerpts of the messages, triggering a criminal investigation by Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy.

## Kwame Kilpatrick’s resignation

Kilpatrick, once a rising Democratic political figure, was charged with multiple felonies arising from the same scandal. In September 2008, he pleaded guilty to obstruction-related charges, agreed to resign as mayor, serve jail time, pay restitution, and give up his law license.

His resignation ended months of political turmoil in Detroit and marked one of the most dramatic municipal corruption scandals in the city’s history.

## Prosecutor’s position

Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy repeatedly emphasized that the case was not about a private affair, but about perjury, obstruction of justice, misuse of public money, and the integrity of the court system. Prosecutors argued that Beatty’s false testimony helped conceal misconduct and contributed to costly litigation and settlement payments by the city.

The prosecution’s position was that public officials must be held accountable when they lie under oath, especially when the lies affect civil litigation and taxpayer money.

## Sentencing terms

Beatty was sentenced in Wayne County Circuit Court to:

- 120 days in jail  
- 5 years’ probation  
- Restitution to the City of Detroit, reported at $100,000  
- Community-service and probation conditions  
- Restrictions intended to prevent her from profiting from the scandal while under court supervision  

Her sentence was less severe than Kilpatrick’s financial obligation, but the court still imposed jail time, rejecting the idea that she should receive only probation.

## Significance

Beatty’s plea confirmed that the text-message scandal was not merely a personal embarrassment for Detroit’s mayor and his chief aide. It became a criminal matter because sworn testimony in a civil-rights lawsuit was false, the city paid millions in a settlement, and officials attempted to suppress evidence. The case helped force Kilpatrick from office and became a defining episode in Detroit’s modern political history.
